title: Study of Training Dynamics for Memory-Constrained Fine-Tuning
claim: A two-stage procedure first selects which layers to train offline, then re-samples channels each epoch online to stay within a fixed memory budget.
layout: 2 main panels, left-to-right: offline layer selection, then online training across epochs, with block arrows and labels beneath them
description: The figure has two framed panels read left to right. The left panel, with a red header reading 'Offline - Layer Selection', shows a small fully connected network. Its layers are grouped by orange and blue shaded bands. Flame-and-snowflake icons below the bands mark which layers are trainable and which are frozen. A large hollow arrow labelled 'On-device deployment' leads to the right panel, which has a green header reading 'Online - Network Training'. That panel shows the same network at 'Training epoch 1' and 'Training epoch 2'. Individual neurons carry flame icons (updated) or snowflakes (frozen), and the edges are colored red or blue to match. Between the two epochs, a second arrow is labelled 'Random channel sampling', and the flame and snowflake pattern changes. A RAM chip with a gauge, labelled B_mem, marks the memory budget. Ellipses imply further epochs. The eye goes first to the flame and snowflake icons on the networks.
caption: TRady dynamically reselects the subgraph to update within the memory budget Bmem.
abstract: Memory-efficient training of deep neural networks has become increasingly important as models grow larger while deployment environments impose strict resource constraints. We propose TraDy, a novel transfer learning scheme leveraging two key insights: layer importance for updates is architecture-dependent and determinable a priori, while dynamic stochastic channel selection provides superior gradient approximation compared to static approaches. We introduce a dynamic channel selection approach that stochastically resamples channels between epochs within preselected layers. Extensive experiments demonstrate TraDy achieves state-of-the-art performance across various downstream tasks and architectures while maintaining strict memory constraints, achieving up to 99% activation sparsity, 95% weight derivative sparsity, and 97% reduction in FLOPs for weight derivative computation.
